why_this_tool: AWS is where the lesson's node provisioning, Spot purchasing and cost attribution decisions are made, so practising against its own purchasing and cost management guidance ties every pod-level scaling choice to the bill it produces.
alternatives: Google Cloud (GKE cluster autoscaler and node auto-provisioning with Spot VMs, billing export to BigQuery), Azure (AKS with KEDA as a managed add-on and Spot node pools), a self-managed Kubernetes cluster with Cluster Autoscaler and OpenCost or Kubecost (no cloud lock-in, but you run the capacity and cost tooling yourself).

setup.do: Read the introduction of the Cost Optimization Pillar and note the practice areas you will apply to an ML inference and training workload.
setup.done_when: You have a one-page note listing the pillar's practice areas with one ML example next to each.

source.title: Cost Optimization Pillar - AWS Well-Architected Framework - Cost Optimization Pillar

setup.why: The pillar gives the vocabulary used in every later step: matching supply to demand, cost-effective resources and expenditure awareness.

setup.do: Sign in to the AWS Management Console with a free-tier account and a non-root user; nothing in this path needs paid capacity.
setup.done_when: The console home page opens for your non-root user and shows the Region you selected.

source.title: What is the AWS Management Console? - AWS Management Console

setup.why: You need console access to see the cost and purchasing screens that the guides describe, even though the workloads themselves run on your laptop.

setup.do: Create programmatic credentials for that user and configure a named profile for the command line interface on your laptop.
setup.done_when: A caller identity check from your terminal returns your user and account number.

source.title: AWS General Reference - AWS General Reference

setup.why: Later steps validate capacity and cost definitions from files, which needs credentials that are scoped and not the root account.

setup.do: Start a local Kubernetes cluster with kind or minikube as the stand-in for a managed EKS cluster, after reading how the managed orchestration options differ.
setup.done_when: The local cluster lists at least one Ready node and you can name the managed option it stands in for.

source.title: Choosing an AWS container service - AWS Decision Guides

setup.why: A managed cluster and its nodes are paid, so a local cluster is the closest substitute for practising pod autoscaling while you keep the AWS capacity model in mind.

steps.do: Write a map of the AWS cost management capabilities, grouping each service under see, plan, optimize or control for an ML platform.
steps.done_when: You have a table that places each cost management service in one group with the ML question it answers.

source.title: Choosing an AWS cost management strategy - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: This is the object model of cost work on AWS: you cannot attribute or reduce GPU and node spend until you know which service answers which question.

steps.do: Compare the EC2 purchase offerings for three workloads: an always-on inference service, a bursty batch scoring job and a long training run.
steps.done_when: Each of the three workloads has a chosen offering and one sentence on the interruption risk you accept.

source.title: Choosing a purchasing option for Amazon EC2 - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: On-Demand, Spot and commitment-based pricing behave differently under interruption and burst, and the right mix is what makes autoscaling cheap rather than just elastic.

steps.do: Write right-sizing criteria for your workload: target CPU, memory and GPU utilization, the request-to-usage ratio you accept, and the review interval.
steps.done_when: A written criteria sheet exists with numeric utilization targets for CPU, memory and GPU.

source.title: Choosing an AWS cost management strategy - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: Right-sizing comes before autoscaling because scaling an oversized pod or node only multiplies the waste; no GPU is needed, use CPU-only requests as the substitute on the laptop.

steps.do: Create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for a small inference deployment on the local cluster, drive load at it, and record replica counts against CPU utilization.
steps.done_when: Replica count rises under load and falls back after it stops, and you have the timeline written down.

source.title: Choosing an AWS container service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is the first scaling layer on any EKS-style cluster, and watching it react shows why correct resource requests from the previous step matter.

steps.do: Configure a KEDA scaler on the local cluster that scales a batch scoring worker on queue depth, using a local queue as the substitute for a managed queue service, and scale it to zero when the queue is empty.
steps.done_when: The worker runs zero replicas with an empty queue and several replicas after you enqueue a batch of messages.

source.title: Choosing an AWS application integration service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: Event-driven scaling follows backlog instead of CPU, which fits bursty ML jobs, and scale to zero is where most of the idle cost disappears.

steps.do: Write a Karpenter node pool definition that mixes Spot and On-Demand capacity across several instance families; real provisioning needs paid capacity, so validate the file with a client-side dry run on the local cluster instead.
steps.done_when: The node pool file passes schema validation and states which workloads may land on Spot and which must not.

source.title: Choosing a purchasing option for Amazon EC2 - AWS Decision Guides

verified.section_found: Hybrid EC2 purchasing strategy: Accelerating workloads with Spot without risking deadlines

steps.why: Node provisioning is the second scaling layer, and a hybrid Spot and On-Demand mix is how deadlines stay safe while most node hours are bought at the Spot price.

steps.do: Configure the workload for Spot interruption: add a disruption budget, graceful termination and checkpointing, then drain a local node to simulate a reclaim.
steps.done_when: After the simulated drain the service stays within its replica floor and the batch job resumes from its checkpoint.

source.title: Choosing a purchasing option for Amazon EC2 - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: Spot savings only hold when an interruption costs seconds rather than a lost training run, so the handling has to be tested before it is trusted.

steps.do: Create a cost attribution scheme: define tags and matching Kubernetes labels for team, model and environment, apply the labels on the local cluster, and choose the cost service that will report on them.
steps.done_when: Every pod in your test namespace carries the three labels and your note names the cost service that reports on each.

source.title: Choosing an AWS cost management strategy - AWS Decision Guides

verified.section_found: Choose an AWS cost management service

steps.why: Cost per team and per model is impossible to reconstruct after the fact, so the tagging contract has to exist before the spend does.

steps.do: Write the queries for GPU utilization and cost per thousand inferences against a sample usage export loaded into a local SQL engine, after choosing which analytics service would hold the real data.
steps.done_when: Your queries return a utilization percentage and a cost per thousand inferences from the sample data.

source.title: Choosing an AWS analytics service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: Idle GPU time is the largest avoidable cost in ML serving, and a unit-cost number is what lets you judge whether an autoscaling change helped; a laptop has no GPU, so use sample metric rows.

steps.do: Write a container task and service definition that splits capacity between Fargate and Fargate Spot through capacity providers, and keep it in version control; do not deploy it, since running it is paid.
steps.done_when: The definition is committed with an explicit base and weight for each capacity provider and a reviewer can read the Spot share from it.

source.title: Architect for AWS Fargate for Amazon ECS - Amazon Elastic Container Service

steps.why: Declaring the Spot mix as a reviewed file is what makes the capacity decision reproducible instead of a console setting someone changed once.

steps.do: Configure usage metric alarms and a monthly budget as code alongside the capacity files, and run a validation of all of them in a local continuous integration job.
steps.done_when: The local pipeline run fails when you break a capacity file on purpose and passes when you restore it.

source.title: Architect for AWS Fargate for Amazon ECS - Amazon Elastic Container Service

steps.why: Automated checks catch a capacity or quota change before it reaches the bill, which is the control half of cost practice.

steps.do: Create a pinned capacity policy document for a production-like setup that combines your pod autoscaling targets, node pool mix, interruption handling, tags and the commitment level for the steady baseline.
steps.done_when: The policy is committed next to the validated files and states baseline, burst and Spot shares with the latency objective each must meet.

source.title: Choosing a purchasing option for Amazon EC2 - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: A working engineer hands over one reviewed policy that says what scales, what is committed and what rides on Spot, so the whole path ends as a decision others can reproduce.
